newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: FORECAST-Yugo dinar at 6 or 7 to the mark in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Yugo dinar at 6 or 7 to the mark in 1997.

text.p: Yugoslavia's dinar could dive as low as six or seven to the German mark by mid-1997 from its current 3.3, the Belgrade-based Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) said on Wednesday.
At the same time, IEN economists cast doubt on the government's calculation of 1997 gross domestic product (GDP), state budget and the size of projected public spending.

"If the GDP is not as large as the government says and if the government again misses growth targets, which is likely to happen, than the projected size of public spending implies the dinar rate between six and seven to the German mark," IEN chief economist Stojan Stamenkovic told reporters.

The government plans a 13 percent rise in 1997 GDP to well over $20 billion, with the budget (federal government administration and defence costs) accounting for 8.94 percent and public spending seen at 47.5 percent of GDP.
But IEN was the first institute to dispute the official estimate of the GDP and said that Yugoslavia's GDP barely stood at $10-11 billion in 1995.

"If GDP does not rise next year, then the budget will not account for 8.94 but for 18-20 percent of the GDP. And we know it cannot be that large, because the Serbian budget alone would be at least four times bigger," Stamenkovic said.
The share of the budget in the GDP will be reduced by inflation and the change in the dinar rate, he added.
A growing number of economists insisted the current dinar rate was unrealistic and said there was no use sticking to it if it did not stimulate exports.
"The realistic rate will allow exporters to operate without losses. Most exporters, mainly the processing industry, cannot cover production costs at the moment," Stamenkovic said.
"But inefficient economy needs a new dinar rate. And it is up to the central bank to intervene on the forex market and steer the rate to what it considers the right level."

Stamenkovic said preserving the dinar rate at the expense of the entire economy was unacceptable. "Monetary authorities should make radical cuts in the country's inefficient economy, but in the meantime firms need to survive."
He insisted economic policy remained deadlocked without radical changes.

"First, there must be restructuring and a sweeping, compulsory privatisation. But until privatisation is carried out, dozens of unprofitable companies must survive. And the change in the dinar rate is their chance to survive," Stamenkovic told Reuters.
Analysts said Yugoslav companies were inefficient because they had to employ twice as many they really needed and to pay huge taxes.
Another economist Mirosinka Dinkic pointed to hidden surplus labour of 500,000 workers. Yugoslavia already has 836,000 unemployed, 26.5 percent of the workforce.
Stamenkovic cautioned it was impossible for any economy to be efficient if 1.6 million employed had to finance 1.3 million persons seeking work plus 1.2 million pensioners.

Dragutin Marsenic, an economics professor, told a seminar: "Let us not play hide-and-seek with the dinar rate. The dinar's true value is far below its current rate and if we want to have exports, we need a realistic rate, regardless of other negative consequences of the devaluation."

IEN director Tomislav Popovic said IEN had suggested to the government it launch a floating rate in June 1994 as a part of overall structural reforms, but there was no response. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
